Shahid Alam, Advocate  -------- For the Petitioner.

Tozammel Hossain  -------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Fatema Khatun and others   -------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
In this Rule a short but important question falls which for determination is whether a transferee of a premises can be added as a party in a suit for ejectment brought by the landlord against the tenants. 

 2. The opposite-party No. 2 instituted Title Suit No. 190 of 1964 against the petitioner for ejectment from the premises in question on the ground of default of rent. The suit was resisted by the petitioner on the ground that on declaration of war between Pakistan and India in September, 1965 the opposite-party became enemy citizen and no suit can be proceeded with at his instance by an application and the learned Munsif by his order dated 27.12.65 returned the plaint and the suit was withdrawn. Against that order the opposite party No. 2 (plaintiff) took Misc. Appeal No. 370 of 1966 to the Court of District Judge, Dhaka. The said appeal, however, was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge leading to filing Second Appeal No. 68 of 1969 in the High Court of Dhaka. The learned Judge allowed the Second Appeal and remitted the suit to the trial Court for disposal according to law. 

 3. The opposite-party No. 1 before me instituted Title Suit No. 131 of 1982 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court Dhaka against the opposite-party No. 2 for specific performance of contract and obtained a decree. The petitioner came to know about the said decree subsequently and filed Title Suit No. 355 of 1983 in the same court of Subordinate Judge for declaration that the decree made in Title Suit No. 131 of 1982 is null and void. 

 4. The opposite-party No. 1 on 11.1.84 filed an application in the Title Suit No. 190 of 1964 under Order 22, rule 10, read with Order 1 rule 10 and section 151 CPC for being added as plaintiff No. 2 in the said suit on the ground that she purchased the suit premises from the opposite-party No. 2 during pendency of the said suit. The said application was resisted by the petitioner on the ground that the alleged document of sale is a fraudulent and collusive document. He further alleged that the transfer is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and decree obtained in Title Suit No. 131 of 1982 by the opposite-party No. 1 was under challenge in the Title Suit No. 355 of 1983. 

 5. The learned Munsif, however, by the impugned order allowed the application and impleaded the opposite-party No. 1 as added plaintiff No. 2 in the Title Suit No. 190 of 1964. 

 6. Mr. Shahid Alam, the learned Advocate seriously challenges the propriety of the order impugned on the ground that in a suit for ejectment against the tenant a subsequent transferee of the premises during pendency of the suit cannot be added as plaintiff inasmuch as the result of the suit will decide his fate. Secondly, the transfer by the opposite party No. 2 in favour of the opposite party No. 1 during the pendency of the suit for eviction is also hit by doctrine of lis pendens under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. He also contends that even if the opposite party No. 1 is made plaintiff, the suit at his instance against the tenant can be proceeded with for want of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this case although the opposite party No. 1 made an application for adding her as plaintiff No. 2 in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 190 of 1964 on the ground of purchase of the disputed premises but there being no tenancy agreement made between her and the petitioner the suit cannot proceed for ejectment without notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act which is a condition precedent. In a suit for ejectment of tenant under the Premises Rent Control Act it is the landlord to institute the suit. In this case the opposite-party No. 1 who is a subsequent transferee of the disputed premises from the landlord during the pendency of the suit cannot be held to be a landlord in absence of any agreement of tenancy made between the petitioner and her. Looking from this angle even if the opposite party No. 1 is impleaded as plaintiff in the Title Suit No. 190 of 1964 still then she will not be able to proceed with the suit. It is to be noticed further that the transfer of the disputed premises during pendency of the aforesaid suit for ejectment is also hit by the doctrine of lis pendens and the result of the suit will decide the fate of the opposite-party No. 1 and in that view of the matter as well the opposite-party No. 1 cannot be said to be a necessary party. The suit for ejectment of the petitioner by the opposite-party No. 2 can very well be adjudicated effectually and completely between the parties of that suit in absence of the opposite-party No. 1. Mr. Shahid Alam has referred me to the decision in the case of Mir Delwar Hossain Vs. Mirza Joynal Abedin Mokhtar, 29 DLR 214 to argue that monthly tenancy cannot be terminated without notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. He also relied upon the decision in the case of Abdul Hafiz and others Vs. Syed Md. Kazem and another reported in 23 DLR 12. In that case in a suit for ejectment of a tenant the question of sufficiency of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act fell for determination by the court. In that case Mutawalli of a Wakf estate served notice determining tenancy of the suit premises in his personal capacity although he filed the suit as Mutawalli of the wakf estate. The court held that the notice was not validly served and was not sufficient inasmuch as the notice was not served by the Mutawalli in the capacity of a Mutawalli. Mr. Alam argued that although there was notice under section 106 served upon the tenant still it was held to be insufficient and on that score the suit failed. He submits that in the instant case this principle of law is very much applicable as there was no notice under section 106 served upon the petitioner by the opposite-party No. 1. In the light of the aforesaid decision I am also of the opinion that where in suit for ejectment no agreement of tenancy exists between the tenant and a subsequent purchaser from the landlord no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act can be served by the transferee of the suit premises upon the tenant and the transferee is not competent to proceed with the suit and he is not a necessary party. A person who is not a party to such an agreement cannot proceed with a suit for ejectment against a person who is not his tenant. In this case there is nothing on record to show that opposite-party No. 1 was the landlord of the petitioner and there was any agreement of tenancy between them. He also referred to the decisions in the case of Sree Nath Paul Vs. Sachindra Kumar Bashu and others reported in 20 DLR 97 and the case of Jamaluddin Vs. Rabeya Begum, 32 DLR 63 to argue that purchase during pendency of a suit is hit by doctrine of lis pendens. In the light of the aforesaid decision I also hold that a transferee who purchases the suit property during the pendency of a suit is not a necessary party in a suit for ejectment and cannot be added as added party under Order 1 rule 10(2) CPC.
